"Let it roll": Article 109 at UNGA80 - Article 109

2 October 2025

## “Let it roll”: Article 109 at UNGA80

The 80 th UN General Assembly High-Level Week – or UNGA80 – has come and gone. The week brought together world leaders, ministers, the media, civil society, advocates, and academics – as well as a small Article 109 delegation! 

At UNGA 80, our team hit the ground running: we hosted events, spoke at others, met with government officials and diplomats, attended discussions on multilateralism to understand what topics are on people’s minds, and met many great people along the way. Overall, we participated in some 40 bilateral meetings, discussions, breakfasts, and receptions across the week.

And yes, the week taught us that you can do both: attend a meeting with a Vice President one minute while learn how to unfold a two-metre banner the next. 

Our sense from the week is that Charter review is seen as a source of hope by many. Throughout the week, various people told us that Article 109 is a solution out of the multitude of crises that the UN – and the world – faces.

Here are our other takeaways from UNGA80! 

### Growing support

Both Kazakhstan and North Macedonia used their General Assembly addresses to call for UN Charter review. The President of Kazakhstan, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, referenced the need to remove out-dated clauses in the Charter and to integrate middle powers in the Security Council. 

The President of North Macedonia, Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, said that youth have the “right” to a renewed UN Charter, to improve the dysfunction of the Security Council, ensure International Court of Justice judgements are implemented, and include modern challenges, such as Artificial Intelligence. 

These countries join India, Brazil, and South Africa (collectively referred to as IBSA), who have repeatedly called for Charter review. On the sidelines of UNGA80, they reiterated this call with a joint statement, referencing global challenges that can be addressed via an Article 109 review conference. 

 Several other world leaders speeches made the case for Charter renewal, even if they didn’t call for it outright. For example, Mia Mottley, the Prime Minister of Barbados, said: “The world needs a reset. We must find, first and foremost, whether we still agree on the same values that inform our Charter.”

Following a bilateral between our Coalition and the Vice President of The Gambia, Muhammad B.S Jallow, keep an eye out for an announcement on their support on invoking Article 109.

This represents a doubling of the number of countries calling for a Charter review conference. 

### For nothing is fixed: launch reception of Article 109

On the Monday, we hosted our official launch reception. Former heads of state, diplomats, civil society leaders, UN officials, journalists and philanthropists were in attendance.

Mary Robinson, former Irish President and Human Rights High Commissioner, delivered the keynote: 

“ The moment has come, and we need to be brave enough to say ‘yes, we do need a UN’ but we need a UN that is fit for purpose, that is at the centre of tackling peace and security, that is at the centre of health issues, that is at the centre of the climate and nature crisis.” 

Our fireside chat featured Helen Clark, former New Zealand Prime Minister and UNDP Administrator; Alexander De Croo, former Belgian Prime Minister; and Ambassador Muhammadou Kah, The Gambia’s Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva.

They provided unique perspectives on why the UN Charter should be reviewed. When asked what it meant for Africa, Ambassador Kah said: 

“It’s about correcting a historical anomaly. For my country, The Gambia, which is a very small country, and for Africa at large, it’s about dignity. It’s about recognition. It’s about agency in shaping the rules of this system that once excluded us.” 

 Alexander De Croo equally touched on his journey from scepticism to being a supporter as he wore our “Article 109er” sticker: 

> “My diplomats used to say that ‘You’re better off with what you have and you never know what you might end up with’ but… it couldn’t be worse than what we have for the moment, at least on the total irrelevance related to the issues that matter.” 

Helen Clark spoke of the fact that we need to meet the moment: 

“We’ve got a common cause here, which is a better international system. So, I just think, let it roll. Move towards that Conference, which should have happened in 1955 and never did.” 

The evening rounded off with Dr. Andrew Forrest’s announcement that Minderoo Foundation has pledged US $1 million to the Article 109 Coalition. In a rousing speech, Dr. Forrest said: “Let’s get rolling with this… if you believe that the dignity of humanity is all that matters.” 

Thank you to Stefan Liebich for hosting us! You can watch a recap of the reception below.

### Town Hall: A Conversation on Renewing the UN Charter 

On the Wednesday, we hosted a Town Hall for our partners, endorsers, and those curious to find out more about Article 109. 

This was a chance to update our network on what we’ve been up to: from building our brand to meetings with various Member States. 

But it was also an important opportunity to come together and discuss where to next for our Coalition. We gathered input on how to engage our network and what to learn from previous coalitions. 

Thank you to all those who attended – and to the Bahá’i International Community for hosting us. 

For anyone not already part of our network: we encourage you to join! 

### Spreading the word

Heba Aly, Article 109’s director, spoke at a discussion convened by the African Union’s Economic, Social and Cultural Council (ECOSOCC). Heba made the case that, as 28% of the UN’s membership is made up of African states, collectively, Africa can make a strong case for Charter review – with the goal of not just requesting a seat at an already broken table, but to lead on building a new one.

We also raised Charter review at the Rockefeller Foundation‘s private roundtable on the future of a principles-based international order. The discussion featured Gordon Brown, the former UK Prime Minister, David Miliband; President of the International Rescue Committee; Comfort Ero, President of the International Crisis Group; Ndidi Okonkwo Nwuneli, President of the ONE Campaign; Linda Thomas-Greenfield, former US Ambassador to the UN and other figures from the world of international diplomacy, government, and philanthropy.

Wrapping up UNGA80, members of our team were at Club de Madrid‘s closed-door discussions. The first focused on democracy and multilateralism, while the second centred on global public goods in a multipolar world. The events kick-started two separate long-term working streams that will feed into the Club de Madrid’s positions on multilateralism. 

It was impressive how many times Article 109 and Charter review also came up in others’ events and in independent discussions! At the International Peace Institute‘s event, that saw the launch of The Elders’ new report on the future of multilateralism, several speakers independently raised the need to review the UN Charter in their opening remarks. 

We also appeared in an opinion piece on Rosa Luxemburg Foundation’s website, in a statement by Democracy Without Borders, several newsletters (including Devex, Global Challenges Foundation and International Intrigue) as well as an hour-long radio programme on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
